chapters.title: Chapter 6: Putting Forex Knowledge to Work

lessons.title: Hedging Explained: How Exporters and Importers Lock In a Rate

children.text: Nilesh runs a ceramic tiles factory in Morbi. A distributor in Dubai has ordered $250,000 of tiles, payable in 90 days. At today's USD/INR of 95.50, the order is worth ₹2,38,75,000, and after clay, gas, labour and freight, Nilesh expects to keep about 8%, roughly ₹19 lakh. But his costs are in rupees and his revenue is in dollars. If the rupee strengthens to 92.50 before he is paid, his profit falls by almost 40%, without a single tile being returned. Nilesh is not a currency trader and does not want to be one. This lesson is about how businesses like his decide what to hedge, how much, with which tool, and how to stop hedging from turning into speculation.

body.text: Hedging is not about beating the market. It is about protecting a business's margin from a risk the business did not choose to take. A good hedge is judged against the rate that keeps the business profitable, not against where the rupee happens to end up.

children.text: Why Currency Risk Hits Margins So Hard

body.caption: Nilesh's $250,000 order with rupee costs fixed at ₹2,19,65,000 (unhedged)

children.text: A 3% move in USD/INR changes Nilesh's profit by almost 40%. That is the core problem for every thin-margin exporter and importer: the currency move is small, but it is applied to the entire order value, while profit is only a small slice of it.

body.title: Nilesh's break-even rate
body.prompt: Nilesh's rupee costs for the order are fixed at ₹2,19,65,000 and he will receive $250,000. Below what USD/INR rate does the order start losing money? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Break-even rate = ₹2,19,65,000 ÷ $250,000 = 87.86. If the rupee strengthened from 95.50 to below 87.86, about 8% in three months, the whole order would lose money. This is the kind of number a business should know before deciding how much to hedge.

children.text: Step 1: Map the Exposure

markDefs.definition: The risk that a specific foreign currency receivable or payable will be worth a different amount in rupees when it is settled.
The broader risk that currency moves change a business's competitiveness and future profits, for example when a stronger rupee makes Indian exports pricier than Vietnamese or Chinese competitors.

children.text: Before choosing any tool, list every foreign currency flow: its currency, amount, direction and date. Most hedging by Indian businesses targets
transaction exposure
, specific invoices and loans.
Economic exposure
is harder to hedge with contracts and is managed through pricing, sourcing and market choices.

body.caption: Common currency exposures in Indian businesses

cells: Morbi tiles sold to Dubai for $250,000
Sell dollars forward, sell USD/INR futures or buy puts
Solar panels imported by a Jaipur EPC firm
Buy dollars forward, buy USD/INR futures or buy calls
A dollar external commercial borrowing by a manufacturer
A bid on an overseas tender not yet won
Options or partial hedges, reviewed when the outcome is known

children.text: Step 2: Use Natural Hedges First

markDefs.definition: An offset built into the business itself, such as dollar costs that match dollar revenues, so that currency moves cancel out without any derivative.
Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency account. It lets exporters keep export earnings in foreign currency in India, to use for later foreign currency payments.

children.text: The cheapest hedge is one that costs nothing. A
natural hedge
matches dollar inflows with dollar outflows. Nilesh imports glazes and spare parts for his kilns and pays for them in dollars. By keeping export proceeds in an
EEFC account
and paying his suppliers from it, he avoids converting dollars to rupees and back, and saves two spreads as well.

body.title: Net exposure
body.prompt: Over the same 90 days, Nilesh will receive $250,000 from Dubai and must pay $90,000 to European and Chinese suppliers of glazes and kiln parts, invoiced in dollars. What is his net dollar exposure to hedge?
body.explanation: Net exposure = $250,000 received minus $90,000 paid = $160,000. The $90,000 is naturally hedged: if the rupee moves, the change in his import cost offsets part of the change in his export revenue. Hedging the full $250,000 would over-hedge, leaving him with an unhedged short position on $90,000.

columns.label: Natural hedges
points: Match dollar receipts with dollar payments
Keep export earnings in an EEFC account
Borrow in the same currency you earn, such as packing credit in foreign currency for exporters
Invoice in rupees where buyers agree, using RBI's rupee trade settlement framework
No derivative, no premium, no margin

columns.label: Financial hedges
points: Cover the net exposure left after natural hedges
Have costs: forward premium or discount, option premium, charges
Need records linking each hedge to a real exposure
Can be sized and timed precisely

children.text: Step 3: Choose the Tool

body.caption: Hedging tools compared for a business

cells: Built into the forward rate, plus bank spread
Any amount and date; cancellation rules apply
Settled at maturity; bank may block credit limits
USD/INR futures on NSE or BSE
Transparent screen price, brokerage and charges
Standard $1,000 lots and fixed expiries; easy to close early
Businesses wanting transparent pricing and flexibility to exit
Uncertain exposures such as tenders, or when upside matters
Tiny exposures relative to margin, or fully natural-hedged flows

stats.label: Documentation relief
stats.context: RBI sets limits below which documents are not required, but the exposure must still exist. Check current limits with your bank

stats.label: Rupee trade settlement
stats.context: RBI framework to invoice and settle trade in rupees

stats.label: Cancel and rebook rules
stats.context: Check current RBI rules with your bank before cancelling a hedge

children.text: Step 4: Decide How Much, and When

markDefs.definition: The share of a net exposure covered by hedges. A 60% hedge ratio on $160,000 means hedging $96,000.
The exchange rate a business uses when pricing orders and preparing its budget. Hedging decisions are often measured against it.

children.text: Hedging is not all or nothing. The
hedge ratio
sets how much protection and how much remaining exposure the business keeps. Many exporters set it against a
budget rate
: if the forward rate available is better than the rate the order was priced at, a high hedge ratio locks in the planned margin.

body.latex: \text{Effective rate} = h \times \text{Hedge rate} + (1 - h) \times \text{Spot rate at payment}
body.caption: h is the hedge ratio, from 0 (unhedged) to 1 (fully hedged)

body.title: Exporter's Effective Rate by Hedge Ratio (3-month forward at 96.19)

children.text: The fully hedged line is flat: certainty. The unhedged line is a straight bet on the rupee. The 50% line sits in between, halving both the damage and the windfall. Many Indian exporters also layer their hedges, covering part of an order when it is confirmed and adding cover in steps, so that the final rate is an average rather than a single timing decision.

body.caption: Nilesh layers forwards on his $160,000 net exposure

body.title: The layered average
body.prompt: Using the table, what is Nilesh's weighted average hedged rate on the $160,000? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Average = 0.50 × 96.19 + 0.25 × 96.40 + 0.25 × 95.90 = 48.095 + 24.10 + 23.975 = 96.17. Layering did not find the best rate, 96.40, or the worst, 95.90. It produced a sensible average without Nilesh having to guess the perfect day to hedge.

body.title: Spot the natural hedge
body.question: Which of these is a natural hedge for a Ludhiana bicycle parts exporter that earns US dollars?
options: Buying USD/INR call options every month
Paying for imported alloy steel in dollars out of an EEFC account holding export earnings
Selling twice the export receivable in USD/INR futures
Converting all dollars to rupees immediately and buying dollars again for imports
body.explanation: Using dollar earnings to pay dollar costs cancels the currency risk on that portion without any derivative and saves conversion spreads. Buying calls would add to a dollar earner's exposure, over-hedging with futures creates a speculative position, and converting back and forth pays two spreads and hedges nothing.

children.text: Step 5: Keep Hedging From Becoming Speculation

body.text: Hedging turns into speculation when the hedge no longer matches the exposure: hedging more than the net amount, keeping a hedge after an order is cancelled, or cancelling hedges to book a profit and then re-hedging at a different rate. RBI's rules require derivatives involving the rupee to be backed by genuine exposures, and in April 2026 it restricted rebooking of cancelled rupee derivative contracts. Keep a written record linking every hedge to an invoice, order or loan.

Every hedger faces hedging regret. If Nilesh sells dollars forward at 96.19 and the rupee then weakens to 99.50, the forward will look like a mistake. It was not. He secured his planned margin, which is what the hedge was for. A business that judges hedges by comparing them with the rate at payment will eventually stop hedging, usually just before the move that hurts it. Judge hedges against the budget rate and the margin they protected.

body.label: A hedge's real benchmark
body.value: The budget rate and the margin it protects
body.context: Not the spot rate on the day of payment. A hedge that delivers the planned profit has done its job, even if the market later offered a better rate.

body.title: A different exposure: hedging a foreign currency loan

children.text: Suppose a Pune auto components maker borrows $5 million abroad for three years because the dollar interest rate looks cheaper than an Indian loan. The saving is an illusion if the rupee weakens over those three years: every repayment costs more rupees. As you learned from interest rate parity in Chapter 2, hedging the repayments with forwards or swaps typically adds a cost close to the interest rate gap, which can eat most of the apparent saving. That is why RBI's rules on external commercial borrowings and many lenders expect significant hedging, and why a foreign loan that only looks cheap unhedged is usually not cheap at all.

body.title: The IT firm that never hedges
body.scenario: A 400-person IT services company in Gurugram earns about $1.5 million a month from US clients, while almost all its costs, mainly salaries and office rent, are in rupees. Its net margin is about 12%. The CFO has never hedged, saying: "The rupee always falls over time, so we only gain by staying open." In the last year, the rupee has weakened sharply, but the company's largest client is negotiating a 5% price cut, and a competitor in the Philippines is bidding for the same work.
body.prompt: Evaluate the CFO's reasoning. Identify the company's transaction and economic exposures, explain the risk of staying fully unhedged, and propose a simple hedging policy.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Transaction exposure: about $1.5 million of monthly dollar receivables against rupee costs. A sharp rupee rally, like the one on 2 April 2026, could cut several percentage points off a 12% margin within weeks.
2. Economic exposure: dollar pricing pressure from clients and competition from the Philippines. A weaker rupee has been helping; if it reverses while prices are being cut, margins get squeezed from both sides.
3. The CFO's reasoning is a long-term bet dressed up as a policy. The rupee's long-run drift is weaker, but the path includes sharp rallies, and a year of losses can happen in between. The company is effectively speculating on the rupee with its operating margin.
4. There is no meaningful natural hedge, because costs are almost entirely in rupees, so financial hedging matters.
5. A simple policy: set a budget rate for the year; hedge on a rolling basis, for example 50% to 70% of the next 6 months of expected receivables and 25% to 40% of months 7 to 12, using bank forwards or exchange-traded futures; review quarterly; never hedge more than expected receivables; and report hedge results against the budget rate, not against the spot rate at maturity.

body.title: A one-page hedging policy for a small exporter or importer
steps: List all foreign currency receivables, payables and loans with amounts and dates.
Net off natural hedges, including EEFC balances and matching payments.
Set a budget rate that keeps each order profitable.
Choose a hedge ratio range and a layering schedule.
Pick tools: forwards for confirmed invoices, options for uncertain ones, futures if transparent pricing and early exit matter.
Never hedge more than the net exposure, and close hedges if orders are cancelled.
Keep records linking each hedge to its exposure and review results against the budget rate every quarter.

body.title: The exporter's currency account
body.textWithBlank: An exporter can keep export earnings in foreign currency in India using an Exchange Earners' Foreign ___ account.
body.explanation: An EEFC account, or Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency account, lets exporters hold foreign currency earnings and use them for foreign currency payments, creating a natural hedge and saving conversion costs.

cards.definition: Currency risk on specific receivables, payables or loans.
The broader effect of currency moves on competitiveness and future profits.
Offsetting foreign currency inflows and outflows within the business, without derivatives.
Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency account for holding export earnings in foreign currency in India.
The share of net exposure covered by hedges.
Adding hedge cover in stages to average the hedged rate instead of timing one decision.

points: Currency moves hit thin-margin businesses hard: a 3% rupee move changed Nilesh's order profit by almost 40%.
Start by mapping every exposure, then use natural hedges such as matching dollar payments and EEFC accounts before any derivative.
Hedge the net exposure, choosing forwards, exchange-traded futures or options based on certainty, cost, cash flow and flexibility.
A hedge ratio and a layering schedule turn hedging into a routine process rather than a market call.
RBI's framework allows hedging of contracted and anticipated exposures, but hedges must stay backed by genuine exposures, and rebooking cancelled contracts was restricted in April 2026.
Judge hedges against the budget rate and the margin they protect, not against the spot rate on payment day.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not hedging, investment, accounting or legal advice. Business figures, forward rates and hedge ratios are illustrative. RBI rules on hedging, documentation, cancellation and rebooking change from time to time. Businesses should agree hedging policies with their bank, auditor and qualified advisers.
